short: Two shots in a Sarajevo street that set the Great Powers marching.
full:
On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, drove through Sarajevo with his wife Sophie. A bomb thrown at the motorcade that morning missed. Later, after a wrong turn brought the car to a halt on Franz Joseph Street, Gavrilo Princip, a nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb of the Young Bosnia movement, fired twice from a few feet away. Both victims were dead within the hour.

Vienna blamed Serbia and, assured of German support, issued an ultimatum on 23 July framed so that it would be refused. Serbia's largely conciliatory reply was rejected and Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July. Russia mobilised in Serbia's defence, Germany declared war on Russia and then France, and the German advance through Belgium brought in Britain on 4 August. Within six weeks a Balkan quarrel had become a continental war. Princip, too young under Austrian law to be hanged, died of tuberculosis in prison in April 1918.
